title_original: Paris Photo: Two Centuries Under Glass
excerpt_original: For its 29th edition, Paris Photo settles under the glass roof of the Grand Palais from November 12 to 15, in step with the Bicentenary of Photography. 246 exhibitors, 38 countries, and around the fair, a whole week of openings, talks and signings spilling across Paris.…

blocks.text: Two hundred years, so what? An anniversary calls for a party, and Paris Photo hasn’t skimped on the candles. For its 29th edition, the fair gathers 246 exhibitors from 38 countries, including 199 galleries and 48 publishers, with 80 newcomers.

“Paris Photo will be the first international event to celebrate the Bicentenary of Photography,” announces Florence Bourgeois, its director. Anna Planas, its artistic director, adds: “This anniversary is not only an opportunity to look back on the history of photography, but also to consider its transformations.”

Right at the entrance, Thomas Ruff sets the tone. Five galleries (David Zwirner, Konrad Fischer, Mai 36, Lia Rumma, Sprüth Magers, no less) have joined forces to unroll 36 meters of hanging, more than forty years of work, from analog photography to digital simulation. Nebulae, portraits, newspapers, pixels. Anna Planas speaks of an installation conceived as an “open book.”

Visitors walk along it more like a station platform, wondering which train to catch. A figure of the Düsseldorf School, Thomas Ruff has the elegance never to choose: for him, a photograph is both a document and a well-mannered lie.

blocks.alt: Red sunset over clouds and sea with a blurred, elongated sun
blocks.caption: From the series “The Skeptics,” 2026 © David De Beyter / Courtesy RVB Books

blocks.text: In the Nave

At the heart of the nave, the Main sector lines up 152 galleries, and the dealers in vintage images hold court. Hans P. Kraus Jr. brings out treasures signed by Louis Daguerre, William Henry Fox Talbot, Anna Atkins and Girault de Prangey, those early practitioners who invented everything without knowing it. Gilles Peyroulet, Bruno Tartarin, Lunn and Serge Plantureux complete the caravan of origins. As Florence Bourgeois points out, “collecting photography today can cover very different realities: a vintage print, a complete series, archives.”

Yet it is in the 44 solo shows that the fair reads best. Merry Alpern’s prying windows, “Dirty Windows,” at Miranda. Stanley Kubrick, a photographer before he was a filmmaker, in the 1950s, at Duncan Miller. Kati Horna at Proyectos Monclova. Clandestine encounters in Bogotá’s movie theaters, captured by Miguel Angel Rojas in the 1970s, at La Cometa.

blocks.alt: Children and a mannequin in front of Chanel display cases, black and white
blocks.caption: From the series “Citizens,” 1979 © Abe Jun / Courtesy The Third Gallery Aya

blocks.text: Pierre Jahan, a make-do surrealist, at Jean-François Cazeau. Malick Sidibé, Bamako’s king of images, at Magnin-A. William Klein at M77, Martin Parr at Rocket (clowning around, as ever). And Isabelle le Minh at Christophe Gaillard, who ties film into knots the way others tie a pastry ribbon. Among the eleven duo shows, Jane Evelyn Atwood and Stéphane Duroy share the in camera booth, two gazes that have never looked away.

Further on, the Voices sector is entrusted to two guest curators, Zasha Colah and Francesco Zanot. “What interests us is what happens when someone brings a perspective different from ours,” explains Anna Planas. Their theme, “La disparition” (Disappearance), starts from a delightful paradox: photography, invented to keep a trace of what fades away, celebrates its two-hundredth birthday just as its own form is slipping away.

blocks.alt: Young man in a denim jacket amid flying sparks under a straw-covered ceiling
blocks.caption: From the series “Wounded Bears,” 2014 © KAI Keijiro / Courtesy The Third Gallery Aya

blocks.text: The curators have gathered images designed to deteriorate or self-destruct, and others that merge into painting or sculpture until they are barely discernible. The metaphor has its limits, and the curators know it. “Considering the genocidal logics at work,” they warn, “this sector focuses on the self-destruction of the image, the recording of its own death and phenomena of disappearance.” Ulay has his solo there, at Charim, a ghost among ghosts.

Next door, the Digital sector has a new captain. Marco De Mutiis, digital curator at Fotomuseum Winterthur, brings together 13 exhibitors around the digital transformations of the image. His observation fits in one sentence: “We no longer ‘see’ through the prism of optics alone.” Photoshop, selfies, facial recognition, the like economy: the eye has changed glasses. And it no longer looks alone: “Our vision is augmented, extended and challenged by machines,” Marco De Mutiis continues.

blocks.caption: “Sunset,” 2026 © Edouard & Bastien Taufenbach & Pourtout / Courtesy Obsession

blocks.alt: Woman in a leotard posing in front of projected stripes and a bodybuilder image
blocks.caption: “Aérobic,” 2026 © Edouard & Bastien Taufenbach & Pourtout / Courtesy Obsession

blocks.text: This year’s guest of honor, the Centre Pompidou, presents “Révéler” (Revealing), around a hundred works by some thirty artists, many of them recent acquisitions, arranged in four chapters: “Faire l’image” (Making the Image), “À l’infini” (To Infinity), “L’atelier” (The Studio) and “Identités” (Identities).
The Cnap, for its part, lines up five works from its collection under a darkroom title, “FIX/DEV.” Fixer, developer: the smell of the trays is never far away.
Upstairs

On the first floor, the Emergence sector brings together twenty monographic projects from nine countries. Here you meet a carpenter napping in his workshop, photographed by Ricardo Cases at Galeria Reus. There is also the destruction of southern Lebanon, rewritten in poetry and calligraphy by Randa Mirza at Tanit. And the bold colors of Marguerite Bornhauser, at Porte B., who turns a net curtain into a blaze and a mesh into snakeskin. The Maison Ruinart Prize goes to Philippe Jarrigeon, presented by Womanray. His series “Le Vrai du Faux” (The True and the False), made this summer in Champagne, casts the Faux de Verzy, those twisted beech trees, as fairy-tale characters. Champagne for the trees.

blocks.caption: From the series “Spectral Matter,” 2026 © Marguerite Bornhauser / Courtesy Poursuite

blocks.caption: From the series “Spectral Matter,” 2026 © Marguerite Bornhauser / Courtesy Poursuite

blocks.caption: From the series “A Lost Place,” 2026 © Aletheia Casey / Courtesy Damiani

blocks.text: The Elles × Paris Photo trail, launched in 2018, is entrusted this year to Aldeide Delgado, founder of WOPHA, under the title “An Oceanic Beginning.” “The sea becomes the starting point for a reflection on how the history of photography can be told,” she explains. The figure speaks for itself: 38% women artists at the fair in 2026, compared with 20% in 2018.

Along the trail, Berenice Abbott at Lunn, Sarah Moon at Howard Greenberg, Susan Meiselas at Magnum. Ishiuchi Miyako at The Third Gallery Aya, Mari Katayama at Suzanne Tarasieve. And Aletheia Casey, at Damiani, whose Australian landscapes look as if they came out of an oven.

At Paris Photo, books naturally have their kingdom along the galleries: 48 publishers from 17 countries, from MACK to Atelier EXB, from Aperture to Chose Commune, and more than 400 signing sessions. One could spend whole days leafing through favorite titles. The Paris Photo–Aperture PhotoBook Awards will be announced on Friday, November 13, at 3 p.m.

On the talks side, the Conversations program gives the floor to Thomas Ruff, Thomas Demand and Zanele Muholi, in dialogue with Tina Campt. Robert Adams, for his part, is recounted by three friends, Sarah Greenough, Mitch Epstein and Jeffrey Fraenkel. Sofia Coppola talks with publisher Michael Mack about the influence of photobooks. Plenty worth listening to.

blocks.alt: Ornate white mirror leaning against yellow-green tiles under a fluorescent tube
blocks.caption: “Mirall,” 2025 © Alba Yruela / Courtesy Chiquita Room

blocks.text: Finally, for the first time, the Prix Pictet enters the nave with Valérie Belin and Alfredo Jaar. Plastic still lifes, a Great Salt Lake drained of life: beauty in the service of an account of ruin.
Beyond the Walls

Paris Photo cannot sit still. A whole constellation of satellites orbits the Grand Palais, and to keep from getting lost, Myrtille Beauvert and Elsa Seignol, founders of the New York agency Signals, have designed a free guide that runs on a phone. A map dotted in navy blue, a personal agenda, a continuously updated listing, and even a filter to keep only one-day events, the ones gone by morning. A pocket compass for a week that has none.

A rundown of noteworthy events. On Wednesday, November 11, from 9:30 a.m., the symposium “Le temps des épreuves” (The Time of Prints), co-organized by the City of Paris department for the preservation of photographic heritage, devotes its final day to the challenges of conservation, at the Musée du quai Branly. At 2 p.m., galerie 24b. opens “P×3 Prix” and “State of the World.” At 7 p.m., the Maison Européenne de la Photographie looks behind the scenes of Irving Penn’s fashion photographs. That same evening, Kometa celebrates its third birthday at Le Consulat Voltaire, until midnight.

blocks.alt: Woman with long hair covering her eyes, seated at a table with a small fish
blocks.caption: From “Passage – de l’ombre aux images” (Passage – From Shadow to Images), 2024 © Sara Imloul / Courtesy Filigranes

blocks.text: Thursday, November 12, is an obstacle course. At 5 p.m., Stephan Vanfleteren opens “Transcripts of a Sea” at Rabouan Moussion. At 6 p.m., Mark Steinmetz hangs “Heure de pointe” (Rush Hour) at Galerie Ithaque, while Rebecca Topakian presents “Concentric Circles” in RosAlma’s Camion-Galerie (a gallery on wheels, someone had to think of it). That same evening, Polka opens two exhibitions, Steve McCurry’s “Immersion” and the ruins of Yves Marchand and Romain Meffre. The Hôtel La Louisiane hosts the fifth edition of Room Service, “The Silent Watchers.”

At 7 p.m., the Fondation Henri Cartier-Bresson leafs through At Night Gardens Grow with Pia Paulina Guilmoth, nocturnal gardens with the moon as the only light. To close the day, at 8:30 p.m., Sofia Coppola is the guest of Chanel’s “7 à 9” at the Jeu de Paume.

blocks.alt: Two long-haired girls among flowers in a garden at night, black and white
blocks.caption: From the series “At Night Gardens Grow,” 2026 © Pia Paulina Guilmoth / Courtesy Stanley/Barker

blocks.alt: Shirtless boy holding a crab by a river, black and white
blocks.caption: From the series “Heart of a Bird,” 2026 © Constance Thalken / Courtesy Stanley/Barker

blocks.text: On Friday the 13th, Polycopies, moored at Port de Solférino aboard the Concorde-Atlantique, hosts Anders Petersen in conversation with David Campany at 4 p.m. The Jeu de Paume schedules two performances, by Davide Sgambaro at 4 p.m. and by Jérôme Grivel at 6:45 p.m.

At 7 p.m., Steve McCurry returns to the MEP for a talk followed by a signing, while Irina Rozovsky discusses her work at Librairie sans titre. In Belleville, Floréal opens “Gangsta’s Paradise” from 6 to 10 p.m., and the Fotofilmic gallery celebrates the launch of JRNL magazine.
Saturday the 14th belongs to books. Le Bal holds its signings from noon to 5 p.m., and Magnum Gallery runs its Magnum Book Festival until 8:30 p.m.

At 3 p.m., Véronique Ellena presents “Mains d’œuvre” (Handiwork) at MAC Créteil. At 3:30 p.m., Maciej Markowicz opens “huit secondes” (eight seconds) at Galerie XII. At 6 p.m., “She Is the Story” takes its final bow at Alta Vista Arts.

blocks.alt: Collage of a red Mini and two tourists at the Cliffs of Moher above a sea of ice floes
blocks.caption: “Viewing the Ice Floes from the Cliffs of Moher,” 1984 © Sean Hillen / Courtesy Momentum

blocks.text: On Sunday the 15th, there is still Adam Rouhana presenting his book at the Grand Palais at 4 p.m., before the nave empties out. And the program doesn’t stop there: the Signals guide lists more than a hundred events over the week. You’ve been warned: you’ll have to choose.

Paris Photo is on view November 12–15, 2026, at the Grand Palais in Paris. 1–8 p.m. (7 p.m. on Sunday), VIP access from 10:30 a.m. Weekday ticket €36, weekend €41, student €26. The Signals Paris Photo Week guide is free and accessible from any smartphone.
